title: The ocean's currents
what: The ocean's currents each month from January 1940 to December 2021, near the surface (1 m) or at 1,500 m, from IAP's gridded geostrophic currents (Cheng and Zhu 2016), drawn as Windy draws the wind: streaks drifting with the water, brighter where it flows faster. Near the surface the Gulf Stream carries the AMOC's warm water north and east across the Atlantic; at 1,500 m its cold water returns south along the deep western boundary off the Americas.
how: IAP gives the eastward and northward current each month on a 1° grid; the site keeps two depths, averages them onto its 1° grid and packs them into images. The streaks are particles moved by the current where they are, read between the grid's nodes, each started again at a random place at sea when it grows old. They move at the same pace on the screen at either depth (14° a second at 1 m/s near the surface, at 0.2 m/s at 1,500 m): the deep currents, a few centimetres a second, are sped up five times. Below that, a streak's pace goes as the square root of its current, so slow water still visibly flows, as Windy draws calm air; brightness tells the speed. After December 2021, the same month of 2021 stands in, said so.
others: These are geostrophic currents: the flow in balance with the ocean's pressure, worked out from its temperature and salinity. They leave out the currents the wind drives directly at the surface, and they cannot be worked out near the equator, where the Coriolis force vanishes, so none is drawn within 3° of it. Before the Argo floats (from about 2005) the deep ocean was sparsely measured and IAP fills it from climate models, so the early deep currents lean on that filling.
